Week Ahead · November 23–27, 2026 · Thanksgiving week

The S&P is standing on its 61.8% line, and the whole week's data lands on Wednesday

The S&P 500 fell 8.6% last week, its worst week since April 2025, and closed Friday at 6,910, 28 points over the 61.8% retracement of the whole March–October run. Nvidia lost 23% on an SEC accounting probe, gold sold off with stocks, and the VIX closed at 35.9. This week has three and a half sessions and almost all of its data on one morning. Here is what I watch, and the five setups I'd study.

The miss first. My locked call for last week was SPY up, holding the $744–745 floor. It broke on Monday and SPY finished at $689.81: 0 out of 3. I read the Fib levels before the 14/30-day direction, which had already turned down on Oct 30. That is now the first thing I check, and it is why every idea below is a put: the S&P's own 14-day is under its 30-day, so the desk rules block new calls. The GOOGL put was a miss too: it fell through its target before the bounce we waited for.

What matters this week
  • SPX on the line: Friday's low (6,882.66) wicked the 61.8% retracement at 6,900.46 and closed at 6,910.39. A hold sets up a bounce toward 7,080; a 15-minute close under 6,880 opens the 78.6% at 6,644.
  • Nvidia's accounting probe: Reuters reported SEC enforcement staff are looking at possible accounting issues. Its 10-Q is due Dec 4. Every AI name trades on this headline.
  • Wednesday 8:30 a.m.: Q3 GDP (second look), October PCE inflation, jobless claims (moved up from Thursday) and durable goods, then the Beige Book at 2:00 p.m. The Fed goes quiet on Saturday.
  • Dell reports Tuesday after the close, the first AI-hardware read after a 19% drop in one week. Workday, Autodesk and HP report the same night.
  • Oil: two tankers were hit near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday after three down weeks for crude. EIA report Wednesday; the OPEC+ group meets Sunday, Nov 29.
  • Holiday hours: closed Thursday. Friday stocks close at 1:00 p.m. ET, bonds at 2:00 p.m. Black Friday on Friday, Cyber Monday on Nov 30.

Gold fell 9% in a week that ended with the VIX at 36. When the oldest panic trade gets sold alongside tech, someone is raising cash, not hiding. Yields fell (the 2-year down 13bp on Friday to 4.63%) while the dollar firmed for a fourth week: that reads as a growth scare plus a scramble for dollars, not an inflation scare. For us it means the selloff is about the AI story itself, not rates, which is why the puts below sit on AI-linked names and why TLT, the one green line, is the only thing that worked.

What's going on

Five forces for a three-and-a-half-day week

1. The AI unwind turned into a trust problem

What we see: Nvidia fell 14.0% on Friday to $125.53 and 22.9% on the week, about $491 billion of value in one day. The chip ETF SMH lost 17.8% on the week; BE −25.8%, CRDO −24.1%, AMD −20.5%, DELL −19.3%. Anthropic's stock (ANT) slipped to $88.91 on its second day, under its $97.17 first close.

Why: Reuters reported on Friday that SEC enforcement staff are examining possible accounting issues at Nvidia. The SEC declined to comment and Nvidia did not respond. The New York Times added Saturday that the probe is early and could end without charges. Nvidia's own CFO commentary on Nov 17 said it plans to file its 10-Q "in the coming weeks"; it is due Dec 4. A valuation scare is about price. This is about whether the numbers can be trusted, and the market sells that first and asks later. I am fairly sure this keeps the AI names heavy until the 10-Q is out.

What would prove me wrong: an early, clean 10-Q, or Dell on Tuesday guiding AI servers higher with no hit to margins. Either would squeeze the AI puts fast.

Names: NVDA, INTC, AMD, SMH, DELL, CRDO, VRT, BE, PLTR, and the AI backers AMZN and GOOGL.

2. A Fed that wants to hike into a correction

What we see: futures price a Dec 9 hike at about 99% (CME FedWatch via Trading Economics). Yet the 2-year fell 13bp on Friday to 4.63% and the 10-year 12bp to 4.92%.

Why: the October minutes (Nov 18) called the hold "a close call", with some officials wanting a hike then; a couple raised a hike bigger than 25bp for December. Governor Waller said on CNBC, "You have to go 50 in December." Barr expects it "will be appropriate to raise rates further." Bonds rallied anyway, which tells me traders think the hikes will slow growth later. Wednesday is the test: core PCE is expected at +0.3% for October, GDP at 3.5%, claims at 201,000. Williams (a voter) speaks Monday at 4 p.m.; the blackout starts Saturday.

What would prove me wrong: core PCE at 0.4% or more. Then the 2-year jumps back toward 4.8% and stocks and bonds fall together, the worst mix for every name we trade.

Names: TLT, IWM, JPM, BAC, HOOD.

For our ideas: the JPM put leans on this force: a hot PCE that lifts short rates while growth slows is the setup that hurt the banks last week (JPM −10.3%). A soft PCE that lets stocks bounce is the bounce the GOOGL, JPM and AMZN puts are waiting to sell. The PLTR, BA and OXY paper puts don't depend on Wednesday.

3. Forced selling, not a credit event (yet)

What we see: the VIX closed at 35.89, its highest since late March, but high-yield spreads widened only 5bp to 3.52%. The equal-weight S&P (RSP) fell 6.2% on the week against 8.6% for the S&P itself. SPY saw an $11.65 billion outflow on Friday.

Why: the crowd was all in going into this. BofA's flow report (EPFR data, week to Nov 18) showed $66.6 billion into stock funds, the seventh straight week of inflows and a record $310 billion over four weeks, with fund-manager cash at 3.6%. AAII bears were 42.2% on Nov 19, before Friday's drop. When everyone is long and the leaders crack, the selling hits the most-owned names hardest, and the rest of the market falls less. That matches RSP beating the S&P.

What would prove me wrong: high-yield spreads pushing toward 4%, which would turn a positioning flush into a credit problem and make the 78.6% at 6,644 likely. The other side: VIX back under 25 says the flush is done.

Names: SPY, QQQ, IWM, and the most-owned names: NVDA, AMZN, GOOGL, PLTR.

4. Oil: three down weeks, then a weekend shot

What we see: WTI closed Friday at $83.98 and Brent at $92.57, crude's third losing week. XOM fell 5.6% and OXY 8.3% on the week, but both bounced Friday.

Why: record flows through Hormuz had been pushing oil down. On Saturday two tankers were hit near Khasab, Oman, and Iran said every ship must coordinate with its authorities (Al Jazeera counts about 25 incidents in a week). That is upside risk for Monday's open. The EIA report comes Wednesday at 10:30 a.m. and the OPEC+ group meets Sunday, Nov 29.

What would prove me wrong: crude opening flat Monday would say the market has stopped paying for Hormuz headlines.

Names: XOM, OXY, XLE help; DAL hurts. The OXY paper put is the one exposed to a spike.

5. The consumer goes into Black Friday in better shape than the market

What we see: consumer staples were the only sector up on Friday (+0.7%). Walmart beat and raised: EPS $0.65 vs $0.64 expected, revenue $188.8 billion, full-year guide $2.84–2.89. October retail sales' control group rose 0.6% vs 0.4% expected, and the University of Michigan's one-year inflation expectation fell to 3.7% from 4.7%.

Why it matters: forecasters expect a decent season. Adobe sees $275.1 billion online for Nov–Dec (+6.7%), Black Friday $12.9 billion (+9.2%) and Cyber Monday $15.1 billion; the NRF sees +4.2%; Mastercard sees +5.5%, about half of it from prices. Best Buy, Dick's, Abercrombie and Burlington report Tuesday morning. If the spending holds while AI cracks, money keeps rotating toward the plain businesses, which is what KO's flat week already shows.

What would prove me wrong: weak Tuesday retail guidance, or Adobe's daily data running under its forecast.

Names: KO, AMZN, SHOP, AAPL.

Every AI-hardware name lost 17–26%. The only green bar is TLT. KO, OXY and XOM lost the least, which is the rotation in one picture.

Lesson of the week

When the realized number lies: one giant day in the window

The desk labels every option CHEAP, FAIR, RICH or EXPENSIVE by comparing its implied volatility (what the option prices in) with how much the stock has actually moved over the last 20 days. INTC's $52.50 put shows IV 92% against 20-day moves of 143%: a ratio of 0.64, CHEAP. That looks like a gift.

It is partly an illusion. Those 20 days include Oct 30, when INTC gapped down 28.6% in one session. That single day inflates the 20-day number. Take it out and the other 19 days move about 86% a year, which puts the same option at 1.08, FAIR. The 60-day number (99%) says the same.

So the rule still lets the INTC put through, and I'm fine with that, because FAIR passes too. But the lesson matters for later: in about two weeks the Oct 30 gap drops out of the 20-day window, the realized number collapses, and the same option can flip to EXPENSIVE overnight without its price changing at all.

The habit: when a label looks too good, look for one giant day inside the window. If there is one, judge the option on the days without it.

AMZN: put the stop beyond the level, not on it

Last week's ask first: the SPX extension ask from Nov 15 is still open. For reference, Friday's SPX low (6,882.66) wicked the 61.8% retracement (6,900.46) of the same Mar 30 → Oct 6 run and closed back over it.

The anchors: your AMZN extension (the Nov 20 set): begin $146.82 (Mar 21, 2022), middle $192.57 (Jul 27, 2022), end $146.82 (Oct 26, 2022). The swing is B − A = $192.57 − $146.82 = $45.75, and every level is C + coefficient × $45.75. You picked the swing from the 2022 move and slid the ladder onto past turning points; the levels count only from the day you drew them.

The math: 2.382 = 146.82 + 2.382 × 45.75 = 146.82 + 108.98 = $255.80, printed $255.79. 2.0 = 146.82 + 91.50 = $238.32. 1.618 = 146.82 + 74.02 = $220.84.

What price did: the 2.382 held as support Nov 16, 17 and 19, then broke Friday (close $246.82). Since you drew your ladders, price has turned within 0.5% of your levels 10 times, mostly within 35 cents. That is the point of the lesson: if your levels attract price that precisely, a stop placed exactly on one gets touched on a normal retest, even when the idea is still right.

Three stops for a put at $245: on the 2.382 ($255.79): $10.79 of risk, 2.2 to 1 to the 1.618. Just beyond it, over the 30-day ($257.10): $12.30, 2.0 to 1. Over Friday's high ($259.97): $14.97, 1.6 to 1. The safer the stop, the worse the trade, and none passes the 2.5 a RICH option needs. So the right stop kills the trade at $245.

The fix is the entry, not the stop. Wait for price to come back up to the band and fail: enter at $254, stop just beyond the band and Friday's high at $260.20. Risk $6.20, reward to your 2.0 $15.68: 2.5 to 1, and 5.3 to 1 to your 1.618. Same levels, same stop logic, a trade that works. That is play 4.

The rule: a stop goes beyond the level and beyond the structure next to it (an average, the last high), by about a third of an ATR (AMZN: $3). If that makes the trade too big, move the entry, never the stop.

Try it on your chart: on GOOGL, where would a stop go for a put entered at $270 if the March low ($271.77) is the level? (My answer is in the plays: $276, beyond both the level and the cluster of Friday-morning candles.)
